name: Skin booster injectables (Profhilo)

lead: Skin boosters are injectable hyaluronic acid products meant to improve hydration and elasticity rather than add volume, for plumper, smoother skin quality. Profhilo, made by IBSA Derma and launched in 2015, is the best-known example and is discussed for crepey or thin skin, including around the eyes.

Hyaluronic acid is abundant in skin and helps keep tissue hydrated. Profhilo is described as a 2 ml syringe of 64 mg non-cross-linked hyaluronic acid, half high- and half low-molecular-weight, said to stimulate collagen and elastin. Published support is described as mostly small open-label studies from 2015 to 2022, some with manufacturer involvement.

paras: Clinicians inject it into the skin, typically as a short series of sessions spaced weeks apart. People use it for overall skin quality and laxity, and it is often paired with other treatments.

Reported effects are mostly mild injection-site reactions such as swelling, redness, bruising, pain and itching, usually resolving within a day or two. Contraindications listed include hyaluronic acid hypersensitivity, bleeding disorders and active skin infection.

angle.text: Skin boosters such as Profhilo are injected to improve hydration and laxity rather than add volume, and are discussed for thin under-eye skin. Better hydration and elasticity give plumper, smoother skin quality. Evidence is mostly small, manufacturer-linked studies.

lead: Skin boosters, or injectable moisturizers, are hyaluronic acid (HA) preparations injected into the skin to improve hydration, elasticity and overall skin quality rather than to add volume. People use them to get plumper, smoother, more luminous-looking skin and to soften the crepey, slack look of the cheeks, neck, hands and around the eyes. Profhilo, produced by IBSA Derma, a unit of the Swiss IBSA group, is the best-known brand and was launched in 2015.[1]

Profhilo uses a hybrid of high- and low-molecular-weight non-cross-linked HA, branded NAHYCO, and is typically injected at a few points per area where it spreads through the tissue.[1][2] A 2026 systematic review of nine studies with 278 participants reported statistically significant changes or trends toward improvement in elasticity, hydration, density, laxity and wrinkle scores across the face, neck, arms, abdomen, hands and knees.[3] Small randomized trials have looked at perioral skin, neck rejuvenation and acne scars.[4][5][6]

Reported side effects are mostly mild, short-lived injection-site reactions, and clinicians describe HA treatments as generally well tolerated.[1][7] Hyaluronic acid is abundant in skin and helps keep tissue hydrated.[8]
infobox: Two sessions about a month apart; results reported for about 4 to 6 months [1]
Not FDA-approved as of January 2026, per Grokipedia [1]

paras: Profhilo is described as a 2 ml syringe containing 64 mg of non-cross-linked HA, split between high- and low-molecular-weight forms, using the maker's NAHYCO technology.[1] It is intended to address skin firmness and laxity rather than add volume.[1]

Clinics offer Profhilo for the cheeks and temples, the neck, the hands and the area around the eyes, and for skin that looks thin or crepey.[1] A 2025 review covers fillers and injectables used to rejuvenate the neck, chest and hands, where demand for rejuvenation has grown.[7]

Claimed benefits include hydration, elasticity and reduced laxity lasting about four to six months, with a standard protocol of two sessions about a month apart.[1] Reported figures include a roughly 29 percent rise in hydration and a 21 percent reduction in neck laxity.[1]

Side effects are mostly mild and short-lived injection-site reactions.[1] Hyaluronic acid fillers generally can cause erythema, itching and, rarely, vascular occlusion.[8] A review of neck, chest and hand rejuvenation describes fillers and other techniques for those areas.[7]

A 2026 systematic review of nine studies with 278 participants reported significant changes or trends toward improvement in viscoelasticity, hydration, density, laxity, Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale and Facial Volume Loss Scale scores, with photographs showing improved turgor, tone and texture.[3] Grokipedia describes the evidence as mostly small open-label studies, some manufacturer-funded, with 11 to 64 participants and a postmarketing figure of over 42,000 patients.[1]

A 2026 split-face, triple-blind randomized trial in 12 women aged 45 to 65 compared Profhilo with saline on the upper and lower lip area at two sessions 30 days apart, assessing skin texture, dermal thickness and perioral wrinkles.[4] A 2022 randomized trial examined botulinum toxin alone or combined with Profhilo gel for neck rejuvenation.[5] A 2024 single-blinded split-face randomized trial in 12 patients tested adding Profhilo to subcision for acne scars.[6] A variant, Profhilo Structura, has been studied for restoring facial fat in a 22-person case series.[9] No studies specific to the under-eye area were found.

timeline.event: Profhilo launched and CE-marked in Europe.[1]
